Dear Salt Lake City Council, I am writing this letter to urge you to not cut the SLCPD budget. I know that political activists have requested the budget be cut. It is unfortunate that this has happened. There is a clear duplicitous nature to this request. One moment ask that police be comprised of better individuals who are better trained, the next they speak about reducing police resources. No doubt if the budget were cut further critic!m would be made that the police are unable to do the job we demand they do. The request reminds me of a child like understanding of politics. Clearly any good institution is self-aware enough to self evaluate and change when needed, accepting input and making appropriate action. That being said it'should be noted that the most vocal critics of the police have always been the criminal elements of society. I remember one such conversation with a wanted Neo Nazi I apprehended where he related an anecdote in which he stated he had been previously shot by federal officers. He stated to me that he felt they should not have shot him because although he had ignored numerous previous commands to drop his firearm, he said was going to drop it. This man, an admitted white supremacist, had a very negative view of police. This is not to say there is not room for improvement. We aught to strive for excellence in our role as guardians of the republic. In order for the Salt Lake City Police department remain a premier police entity, we must be appropriately funded. In order to recruit the best people we must be able to compensate well. Right now officers are required to meet POST's minimum of 40 hours in service training every year. We aught to get more training, training costs money. If we intend to have the best officers who respect citizen rights better than other agencies, we cannot cut the budget. One thing should be noted, Salt Lake City Police has a good reputation in the community. I cannot tell you how many people have expressed to me that they feel SLCPD is tops! This reputation is gained by the resources devoted to our department, and it is a reflection on the city council's good decisions to appropriately fund the police. The reputation is also gained by accountability, which is very present in our department. Another thing that has made Salt Lake City Police such a well respected institution is our response to crime in our jurisdiction. Notably SLCPD's response to the Trolley Square shooting is regarded as influential toward modernizing the active killer response throughout the nation. SLCPD I'vestigated Lori Hacking?s murder and apprehended the killer, Mark Hacking. SLCPD's response to Mackenzie Lueck murder was exemplary, apprehending and charging the perpetrator quickly. This removed a dangerous subject from the community. Without the appropriate resources these incidents could not have been addressed appropriately. Finally I plead with you to maintain our SLCPD budget so that Salt Lake City can remain autonomous. Budget cuts will no doubt have consequences. The State of Utah looks very closely at Salt Lake City as the State Capital, and a political subdivision of the state. In years past the State Legislature has not been shy about passing laws to address policies they dislike in Salt Lake City. I fear that budget cuts toward the essential service of the Police Department will invite the State to further remove authority from the city to maintain its autonomy. Let our rally cry be DEFEND rather than defund! It is time to eschew policies that make the citizens and police less safe. This is my plea to you, concerning our budget. Now I?d like to provide you with some of my experiences as a police officer here in the city. I have literally shed blood, sweat and tears for this Salt Lake City community. I remember as a new officer reading the suicide note of indigent mother, she had taken pills. We found her unresponsive and she was transported to the hospital. I shed tears when I read that she had decided to take her own life after DCFS had taken her kids. I remember on a Christmas Eve, a 12 year old shot himself in the head in front of his father during an argument. I arrived while the Fire Department tried desperately to help this kid. I remember the thick bright red blood. I did my best to console a grieving father, to no avail. That Christmas Day, I heard from sanctimonious family members who insinuated horrible things about the police. I was there when a wife had found evidence that her husband was abusing their nieces. After we arrested the suspect. I witnessed an officer offer a hug to this distraught woman, her psyche shattered by the trauma of the day. I saw her sob on his shoulder. I've consoled the survivors who found their family member dead, from suicide, overdose or old age. I've arrested more spouse abusers than I could ever remember. I've found children, small children who found their way out of the house onto the city'streets, to runaways who left their parents in anger. I have been assaulted numerous times by criminals unwilling to face the consequences of their own actions. I have rushed to the aid of officers and citizens who were dealing with dangerous criminals. I've confronted armed criminals. I remember speaking with a pregnant victim at the hospital, she had a high risk pregnancy and she was scared because she had been raped. I tracked the suspect down, and apprehended him. We found Probable Cause and he was arrested. He is in prison today for that rape. I've plead with countless drug addicts on the way to jail. I've admonished them to change their lives. I've provided information on resources and how to get help. I remember the gratitude and also the indifference. I've purchased groceries for a struggling mother. I've watched my wife struggle with the lies told and accepted about police officers. I've felt the love of a grateful community, but I've also felt the disdain of citizens who?ve prejudged me. I've heard from citizens who told me their lives were saved by other police officers. They thanked me, for my association with such officers. I've shared the pain of every victim. I've recognized the perpetrators as humans, with human rights and human dignity. I can say without reservation I've upheld my oath of office. Thank you for your consideration, Respectfully, David Campbell.

Dear Mayor Mendenhall, Rep. Wharton, and the rest of the City Council, I appreciate your consideration and work in this stressful, fast-paced moment. I know you're under tremendous pressure from many different constituencies. I also know that the phrase 'defund the police' sounds alarming and radical. I quickly wanted to make sure you were aware that the idea is not as radical as it sounds. Another way to look at it is that we've put far too much burden on our police departments. If as a society we better funded our social support networks, education systems, and healthcare systems, a lot of our policing needs would disappear, and would be replaced by a more just, enjoyable, and prosperous society for all. This may sound pie-in-the-sky, but the data shows that police departments do not achi've their intended goal, and simply balloon in cost while creating more incarceration costs as a result. I would rather spend that money positively than defensively and ultimately, destructively. Think of defunding the police as a goal that our spending can shape an evolution toward. I think this CNN article does a good job of outlining the concept, while avoiding advocacy or bias: https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/06/us/what-is-defund-police-trnd/index.html Instead of looking to policereform (which doesn't work <https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2020/may/31/the-answer-to-police-violence-is-notreform-its-defunding-heres-why> ), instead focus on how we can extricate police from elements of law enforcement where they aren't needed, and have actual qualified workers and functional systems take care of those problems. I'll provide two examples in traffic violation and mental health/social health response. In either case, armed enforcement creates more issues than it solves. It is true that sometimes responding to these situations escalates to where violent enforcement is required. But in that case, there are simple solutions. In traffic and transportation, simply remove the process where routine traffic stops involve criminal history checks, and you'll never have to worry about ticketing officials getting hurt in the line of duty. Fishing for warrants from broken tail lights is an incredibly inefficient and unjust way to deal with crime and drug trafficking, anyway. For motor vehicle violators who are non-compliant, we could record their behaviour and use our already robust tracking and identification systems around motor vehicles to follow up and enact fines, remove licenses, or impound vehicles. In short, city employees with cameras, not guns, could do the vast majority of transportation-related police work better than our current militarized law enforcement. For mental health, substance abuse, and education/youth based issues, social workers should be the first responders, not police. They could be educated and prepared to intervene in an informed matter and de-escalate situations when possible. In both traffic enforcement and mental health response, first contact workers could 'escalate' calls to a smaller armed police department in the event of a real dangerous emergency, but the aforementioned steps would minimize these encounters rather than exacerbate them. The idea that one officer should be qualified to respond to a emotionally distraught teenager, a schizophrenic having a bad day, a civil protest, and a violent criminal is unrealistic. Instead of overburdening that (police) system and increasing its already bloated budget, why aren't we educating our youth and providing state and federal resources for people in need? I strongly urge you to think boldly and creatively in this decisive moment. We could be a city that moves toward a better future for all American citizens, instead of doubling down on the fear that has created an unjust system for many. Thank you, Davey Davis

Most Black residents, residents of color, and LGBTQ residents have witnessed the violence and carelessness of the police here-they are violent in the face non-violence and peaceful protesting. Respectfully, change will only happen if money is allocated towards resources which will help communities thrive and heal, rather than face unnecessary violence, hostility, and tension. Our communities deserve better than this. If the Salt Lake City government claims to care about its residents of color, they should directly address this fixable issue. Our libraries, housing, transit, social welfare programs, and community centers are in dire need of financial and tangible support. We've seen Salt Lake City take wonderful action in the past to support its residents, and now is an important time to continue this trend. How can we allocate funding towards community and transformative justice? How can we help Black residents feel safer in their own streets? Police brutality and lack of accountability for the police should be centered in the conversation. I send this message with love and hope for all of Salt Lake City. Dan, I want to offer my opinion as you, the city council, and the mayor try to decide on a proper course of action related to police oversight and funding. Local and national events only serve to strengthen my belief that we need to force significant change in the way police conduct themselves. While police officers act honorably during the vast majority of interactions, I see way too many instances of brutality and seeming indifference. We need to improve. We need oversight. Where might we focus our efforts? I have some ideas. First, we should de-emphasize militaristic types of response. Police departments seem to have amassed abundant stocks of riot control equl'ment. There certainly is a time and place for this equl'ment. That time does not include peaceful protest. Waves of officers marching in show-of-force tactics employing tear-gas, rubber bullets, billy clubs, shields, helmets, and body-armor serve to incite fear needlessly and to destabilize what very-well might otherwise be peaceful groups of protesters. I recognize that the police force may need to have a small- or moderately-sized squad outfitted in riot gear, ready for rapid insertion. But to make that first move - showing a massive, intimidating force before riotous behavior begins - can lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy. I recognize that we need to be able to protect officers. But we also need to police in a way that serves, rather than inflames the community. What oversight steps could we take? We could start by structuring civilian oversight for the use of aggressive types of riot-control equi'ment. * Naturally, swat teams would face less restrictive control upfront. * Make clear to the police chief that the Department'should not lead with riot gear and tactics when we expect mostly peaceful protests. * Have the chief submit recommendations to the city council for situations in which escalation to riot gear and tactics would automatically be allowed. Have the city council work with the chief to codify pre-approved guidelines. * For situations below the level where riot tactics are pre-authorized, but for which the police chief wants pre-approval, (s)he would need to seek advance authorization from a civilian supervisor (such as the mayor or the city council). Next, I would like to mandate and incentivize knowledge useful in de-escalation techniques. It is clear to me that we need to mandate training in this regard. I envision lots of officers, and even instructors, rolling their eyes as we force them to attend this type of training. * I'm pretty sure that you and I both saw this adverse reaction during mandated training as military pilots. But I have also seen that attitudes can change with the right buy-in, delivered in a top-down manner, extending through city council, the police chain of command, training officers, and finally, officer mentors. * Specifically, cockpit resource management (CRM) is an industry term that airlines (and mirrored in medical operating rooms) have adopted. This valuable managerial technique took years before receiving widespread buy-in. It is now an indispensable tool that greatly increases safety throughout all phases of flight and in operating rooms across the nation. * The broad police culture needs to emphasize community service and non-violent problem-solving. It won't happen overnight, but with the right support throughout various civilian and police leadership levels, it can happen. * Incentivize further education in highly-desired degrees teaching non-violent problem-solving (such as social work, psychology, etc.). * Budget funds for officers to attain these degrees in their off time. Mandate that officers who benefit from these programs will need to pay back the community by staying on the force for some specified period. * Increase promotional opportunities to those with these desired degrees. * Increase officer pay by some percentage for those with these desired degrees. Finally, I think the mayor and city council should exert tight control over any funds used to purchase military-style equi'ment. Once again, I recognize that our police department needs this type of equi'ment. But we should not be so flush in these tools that we i'mediately turn toward their use without first availing ourselves of less-inciting and less lethal techniques.

Treasa Stewart

City Council, Please do not disregard this; it is not an attack on you, it is a cry for your help. It has come to my attention that during this extreme time, we have faced earthquakes, pandemics, incidents of unjust actions from officers not belonging to your City, riots leaving officers injured (some of these injuries being permanent), and an Officer Involved Critical Incident. It has been tiring for everyone in this country, this state, this city, and this police department. Officers and civilians have been working long hard hours, and the risk has become almost unbearable. I have risked my life from exposure to COVID-19 from one call to the next for this city. I have risked bodily injury, and have been permanently injured from violent fugitives in the line of duty. I have been assaulted off-duty and had a violent offender fight me for my gun, unprovoked. I have risked my life standing in a thin blue line from violent protesters that were able to turn your city into a war zone. Dangerous items such as rocks, hatchets, street signs, maintenance hole covers, skateboards, baseball bats, etc. were hurled by violent rioters who were chanting that they wanted your police dead. This resulted in 26 officers who reported injury to the city, not counting other injuries that went unreported. Several officers were hurt that stood there for many hours, and still protected the city you represent. Officers risk their life day-in and day-out, answering the calls that no one else will. Officers respond to civil disputes, domestic disputes, threats with a gun, etc.,and unfortunately sometimes it results in taking a life to stop the threat to the officers and the public, especially when several people had already been threatened with a gun, the gun pointed at their heads, one victim being hit across the face with the gun, all while being robbed. The existing ten-day release of body camera video does not breed transparency, but actually paints a whole I'vestigation, which takes several months, into five minutes. This is unjust to officers who protect your city, who were in a life or death situation with a man with a gun and pointed it at them, the full detail of which is not depicted in the short press release. The men and women in Blue, who are highly professional and well trained, protect this City at all cost, even if this cost is their own life. I understand your position is to hear the complaints from the city residents, city business owners, and city employees, as doing so is part of your job. I also understand that the ones who appreciate the police have been vocally accepting of us and have thanked us (myself included) every day we are out on the street. They understand that this job is hard; it's dirty and sometimes forces you to make life-altering decisions based on the behavior of violent criminals. They often tell me that they appreciate that we wear this badge, and risk our lives so that they do not have to. This is often forgotten, especially when there hasn't been an officer death in Salt Lake City since way before the election of the current administration. Salt Lake City Police Department is an exceptional department that deals with violent crimes more than other cities in Utah. This, in turn, means there is more likelihoodof an officer-involved critical incident than in other areas. It is only fair that you do not decide where you stand until you have the full story of the OICI, just as it would only be fair to assess the efficacy of our elected officials on their entire term and not on one negative incident. Officers come to Salt Lake City Police Department for the professionall'm, opportunity, and compensation for their greater exposure to risk than in other areas of the state. With all the information above, I implore you to not cut the police budget. If the police budget is cut, you can expect the following as a result: inadequately trained officers, inadequately equipped officers, underpaid officers, and ultimately, good officers leaving this department. Food for thought, your city only survived this last week because your officers fought by themselves, even though the odds were against them. Your officers fought while outside agency officers from around the state responded, not to protect this city, but to fight with our officers who were fighting an evil they could not defeat on their own. This adds extreme liability to your city, for which you are culpable as its city council. Now, imagine if you did not have the equi'ment, you did not have the manpower, and you did not have the dedication of your current police department to protect this City. Our city would be unrecognizable, and might more closely resemble the chaos of Minneapolis over the past week, consumed by fire and anarchy. I understand some of you have families; I too have a family. I have two three-year old children and a wife at home, whom I kiss and say, see you soon, knowing I'may not come home. To be honest, the risk not seeing them again is overwhelming as it is, with potential funding cuts making that risk even more difficult to abide. I beli've that the Salt Lake City Police Department is the best in the state and best in the country. Do not ruin us, and please, do not abandon the city that we love by robbing its protection. With an aching heart, Tyler Norman
